notes.subtitle: Common Factors, Common Multiples, HCF & LCM

concepts.title: Factors and multiples
concepts.text: Factors divide a number exactly. Multiples are the times table of a number.

concepts.title: HCF: the biggest equal group
concepts.text: HCF = the largest number that divides all the given numbers. It answers 'biggest equal group' questions.

concepts.title: LCM: when do they meet again?
concepts.text: LCM = the smallest number that all the given numbers divide. It answers 'next time together' questions.

concepts.title: The prime-factor shortcut
concepts.text: HCF: shared primes with the smaller powers. LCM: all primes with the larger powers.

practice.question: Two numbers have HCF 4 and LCM 72. One is 24. Find the other.
Three ropes 64 m, 80 m, 96 m are cut into equal pieces of greatest length. Find the length and the number of pieces.
Traffic lights change every 48 s, 72 s and 108 s. They change together at 7:00 a.m. When next?

notes.intro: Anu's class is packing gift boxes: 48 apples, 72 oranges and 96 bananas, with the same number of fruits in every box. And two runners on a track want to know when they will meet at the start again. Both puzzles are about finding common ground between numbers.

lessons.title: Factors and multiples
lessons.story: Anu arranges 12 chairs in equal rows: 1 row of 12, 2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4, … Ravi counts in 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16 …
text: The factors of 12 are the numbers that divide 12 exactly: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. They are the possible row sizes.
The multiples of 4 are the numbers in the 4 times table: 4, 8, 12, 16, … A number has a few factors but endless multiples.

picture.caption: Factors divide a number. Multiples are made from it.

think.question: List the factors of 18.

lessons.aha: Factors divide a number exactly. Multiples are the times table of a number.

lessons.title: HCF: the biggest equal group
lessons.story: Anu has 12 red and 18 blue balloons. She wants to make bunches with the same number of balloons in each, and all balloons used, one colour per bunch. What is the biggest bunch size?
text: The bunch size must be a factor of 12 and a factor of 18: a common factor. Common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
The biggest one is 6. This is the Highest Common Factor, HCF(12, 18) = 6. She makes 2 red and 3 blue bunches.

picture.caption: The largest common factor is the HCF.

think.question: Find the HCF of 36 and 48.

lessons.aha: HCF = the largest number that divides all the given numbers. It answers 'biggest equal group' questions.

lessons.title: LCM: when do they meet again?
lessons.story: Asha runs one round in 6 minutes and Bina in 8 minutes. They start together. When are they next at the start together?
text: Asha is at the start at 6, 12, 18, 24, … minutes (multiples of 6). Bina is there at 8, 16, 24, … (multiples of 8).
The first common time is 24 minutes. This is the Lowest Common Multiple, LCM(6, 8) = 24.

picture.caption: The first time both are at the start is minute 24.

think.question: Find the LCM of 4 and 6.

lessons.aha: LCM = the smallest number that all the given numbers divide. It answers 'next time together' questions.

lessons.title: The prime-factor shortcut
lessons.story: For big numbers like 84 and 90, listing factors takes too long. Thatha shows Anu a factor tree.
text: Break each number into primes: 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 90 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5.
HCF: take the primes they share, as many times as both have them: 2 × 3 = 6. LCM: take every prime the greatest number of times it appears: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 1,260.

picture.caption: 84 = 4 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. The gold circles are primes.

think.question: For two numbers, check that HCF × LCM = the product.

lessons.aha: HCF: shared primes with the smaller powers. LCM: all primes with the larger powers.

lessons.title: A quick ladder and some patterns
lessons.story: Thatha shows Anu a fast way to find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18 together, in a 'ladder'.
text: Divide both numbers by a prime that divides both: 2 → 6 and 9. Then 3 → 2 and 3. Stop when no prime divides both.
HCF = the primes on the left: 2 × 3 = 6. LCM = the left primes × the numbers at the bottom: 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 = 36.

Patterns: the HCF of two consecutive numbers is 1. For co-prime numbers, LCM = product. If one number divides the other, the HCF is the smaller and the LCM is the larger. The HCF always divides the LCM.

picture.caption: Ladder method: HCF = 2 × 3 = 6; LCM = 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 = 36.

think.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 9 and 10 without working.
think.answer: They are consecutive, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 90.

lessons.aha: Ladder: divide both by common primes. HCF = left primes. LCM = left primes × bottom numbers.

lessons.title: HCF or LCM? Reading the question
lessons.story: Ravi always mixes them up. Thatha gives him a trick: listen to the question's words.
text: HCF words: 'largest', 'greatest size', 'equal groups', 'tiles', 'boxes', 'cut into equal pieces'. The answer is SMALLER than (or equal to) the numbers.
LCM words: 'next time together', 'smallest number divisible by', 'bells ring together', 'lights change together'. The answer is BIGGER than (or equal to) the numbers.
For remainders: the smallest number that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 6, 8 and 10 is LCM + 2 = 120 + 2 = 122.

picture.caption: The words in the question tell you which to use.

think.question: Three bells ring every 12, 15 and 20 minutes, together at 8:00. When next?

lessons.aha: Splitting into equal parts → HCF. Meeting again → LCM.

examples.question: Largest square tile for 360 cm × 600 cm.
Smallest number leaving 2 when divided by 6, 8, 10.

mistakes: Using LCM for a 'largest size' question.
Taking larger powers for HCF.
Forgetting to add the remainder.
Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers (it works only for two).
checklist: Write the prime factorisation in index form.
State HCF or LCM before calculating.
Answer in the units of the question.
Check that the HCF divides each number.

notes.subtitle: Multiplying & Dividing Decimals

concepts.title: Sliding the point
concepts.text: × 10ⁿ: move the point n places right. ÷ 10ⁿ: move it n places left.

concepts.title: Multiplying decimals
concepts.text: Multiply as whole numbers, then give the answer as many decimal places as the question has altogether.

concepts.title: Dividing decimals
concepts.text: Move the point in both numbers by the same number of places until the divisor is whole.

concepts.title: Fractions that stop and fractions that repeat
concepts.text: In lowest terms, a denominator with only 2s and 5s gives a terminating decimal; any other prime gives a repeating one.

method: Place the decimal point by counting places.
For division, make the divisor whole first.

practice.question: A pen costs ₹7.75. Find the cost of 24 pens.
How many 0.25 L glasses from 7.5 L of juice?
A car uses 6.4 L of petrol for 89.6 km. Find the distance per litre and the petrol for 210 km.

notes.intro: Thatha fills 12.4 litres of petrol at ₹102.50 per litre. 'What is the bill?' he asks Anu. Then he cuts a 9.6 m ribbon into 0.32 m pieces.
before: know place value after the decimal point

lessons.title: Sliding the point
lessons.story: Anu multiplies 2.5 × 10 and gets 25. Then 2.5 × 100 = 250. 'The digits stay the same. Only the point moves!'
text: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit 10 times bigger, so each digit moves one place left: the point moves 1 place right. × 100 moves it 2 places, × 1,000 moves it 3 places.
Dividing moves the point to the left: 3.7 ÷ 100 = 0.037.

picture.caption: 2.5 × 100 = 250: each digit moves two places to the left.

lessons.aha: × 10ⁿ: move the point n places right. ÷ 10ⁿ: move it n places left.

lessons.title: Multiplying decimals
lessons.story: Anu finds 0.3 × 0.2. Ravi says 0.6. Anu draws a picture.
text: 0.3 is 3 tenths and 0.2 is 2 tenths. In a 10 × 10 square, 3 tenths of 2 tenths is 6 small squares out of 100, that is 0.06. Ravi was wrong.
Quick method: multiply as whole numbers (3 × 2 = 6), then count the decimal places in the question (1 + 1 = 2) and put that many places in the answer: 0.06.

picture.caption: The gold overlap is 6 out of 100 small squares.

lessons.aha: Multiply as whole numbers, then give the answer as many decimal places as the question has altogether.

lessons.title: Can multiplying make a number smaller?
lessons.story: Ravi multiplies 8 × 0.5 and gets 4. 'Multiplication made it smaller! Is my calculator broken?'
text: No. Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes the answer smaller: 0.5 is a half, so 8 × 0.5 = 4. Multiplying by 1 keeps it the same. Multiplying by a number more than 1 makes it bigger.
Division works the other way: dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger. 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12, because twelve halves make 6.

picture.caption: × less than 1 → smaller. × more than 1 → bigger.

think.question: Is 45 × 0.9 more or less than 45?
think.answer: Less, because 0.9 is less than 1 (it is 40.5).

lessons.aha: × a decimal less than 1 makes smaller. ÷ a decimal less than 1 makes bigger.

lessons.title: Dividing decimals
lessons.story: Thatha cuts a 9.6 m ribbon into pieces of 0.32 m. How many pieces?
text: Dividing by a decimal is hard, so first make the divisor a whole number. Multiply both numbers by 100: 9.6 ÷ 0.32 = 960 ÷ 32 = 30 pieces.
This does not change the answer, because both numbers grow by the same factor, like sharing 960 paise instead of ₹9.60.

picture.caption: Make the divisor a whole number first.

lessons.aha: Move the point in both numbers by the same number of places until the divisor is whole.

lessons.title: Long division with decimals
lessons.story: Anu shares 7 rotis equally among 4 friends. Each gets more than 1 roti, but how much more?
text: 7 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 3. Put a decimal point and add a zero: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2. Add another zero: 20 ÷ 4 = 5. So 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75.
Sometimes the remainders repeat forever: 2 ÷ 3 = 0.666…
Special divisors: ÷ 0.1 = × 10, ÷ 0.5 = × 2, ÷ 0.25 = × 4. If the divisor is halved, the quotient doubles.

picture.caption: Add zeros after the decimal point and keep dividing.

think.question: Find 9 ÷ 0.25 in your head.

lessons.aha: Keep dividing by adding zeros after the decimal point. ÷ 0.5 means × 2.

lessons.title: Fractions that stop and fractions that repeat
lessons.story: Anu changes 3/8 into a decimal: 0.375. It stops. Then she tries 1/3: 0.3333… The 3s never end!
text: To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the top by the bottom. Sometimes the division ends (terminating decimal). Sometimes a digit or group repeats forever (repeating decimal).

The secret is in the denominator (in lowest terms). If its only prime factors are 2 and 5, the decimal stops, because it can become 10, 100, 1,000 … Otherwise it repeats. 7/20 = 35/100 = 0.35 stops; 5/11 = 0.4545… repeats.

picture.caption: Only 2s and 5s in the denominator → the decimal stops.

think.question: Does 1/6 terminate?

lessons.aha: In lowest terms, a denominator with only 2s and 5s gives a terminating decimal; any other prime gives a repeating one.

lessons.title: Money and measurement problems
lessons.story: Thatha's petrol bill: 12.4 litres at ₹102.50. Anu estimates first: about 12 × 100 = ₹1,200.
text: Exact: 102.50 × 12.4 = 1,271. The bill is ₹1,271, close to the estimate, so the answer makes sense.
Always estimate first. If your exact answer is far from the estimate, check the decimal point.

picture.caption: Estimate, calculate, then compare.

think.question: A pen costs ₹7.75. Find the cost of 24 pens.

lessons.aha: Estimate first; it catches a misplaced decimal point.

mistakes: Wrong number of decimal places in a product.
Moving the point in only one number when dividing.
Thinking every fraction gives a terminating decimal.
Not checking with an estimate.
checklist: Show the count of decimal places.
Write money to two places.
Use a bar for repeating digits if you can.

notes.subtitle: Statistical Questions, Mean, Median & Range

concepts.title: Questions with many answers
concepts.text: A statistical question expects answers that vary.

concepts.title: The mean: sharing equally
concepts.text: Mean = total ÷ number of values. It is the 'fair share' value.

concepts.title: The median: the middle one
concepts.text: Order the data first. The median is the middle value; one extreme value cannot move it much.

concepts.title: Range: how spread out?
concepts.text: Range = highest − lowest. A small range means consistent data.

method: Find the sum and count for the mean.
Find the middle for the median.
Find max − min for the range, and interpret.

practice.question: Is 'What is your shoe size?' asked to the whole class a statistical question?
The mean of 6 numbers is 15. One number 30 is removed. Find the new mean.
Marks: 35, 40, 38, 95, 37. Which is better, mean or median? Find both.
Find x if the mean of 4, 7, x, 9 is 7.
Heights (cm): 142, 150, 138, 155, 147, 150. Find the mean, the median and the range.

notes.intro: Anu's class wants to know: who is more consistent, batter A or batter B? Which town has costlier onions? Questions like these are answered with data.
before: add and divide numbers, including decimals

lessons.title: Questions with many answers
lessons.story: Ravi asks, 'How tall is our teacher?' Anu asks, 'How tall are the students in our class?'
text: Ravi's question has one answer. Anu's question has many different answers, because heights vary from student to student. A question that expects varied data is a statistical question.
To answer it, we collect data and describe it with a few numbers: a typical value and a measure of spread.

picture.caption: Heights of 10 students (cm): the values vary, so we need statistics.

think.question: Is 'What is your shoe size?', asked to the whole class, a statistical question?

lessons.aha: A statistical question expects answers that vary.

lessons.title: The mean: sharing equally
lessons.story: Shreyas bounces a ball on his bat in 8 tries: 6, 2, 9, 5, 4, 6, 3, 5 bounces. 'What is my usual score?'
text: Imagine pouring all the bounces together and sharing them equally among the 8 tries. Total = 40. 40 ÷ 8 = 5. The mean (average) is 5.
If you know the mean and the number of values, the total is mean × number. Use this to find a missing value.

picture.caption: Levelling the bars to the same height gives the mean, 5.

think.question: The mean of five numbers is 12. Four are 10, 14, 9, 15. Find the fifth.

lessons.aha: Mean = total ÷ number of values. It is the 'fair share' value.

lessons.title: The median: the middle one
lessons.story: Seven friends get pocket money: ₹50, 60, 55, 300, 65, 45, 70. The mean is about ₹92. 'But nobody except one gets that much!' says Anu.
text: Arrange the values in order: 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 300. The middle value is ₹60. This is the median.
For an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. The median is not pulled up by one very large value, so here it describes a typical friend better than the mean.

picture.caption: (300 is far off the scale.) The middle value is 60.

think.question: Find the median of 25, 24, 26, 28, 30, 35.

lessons.aha: Order the data first. The median is the middle value; one extreme value cannot move it much.

lessons.title: Mean or median: which to use?
lessons.story: Two shops sell onions. Anu writes the monthly prices for each shop and must say where onions are usually cheaper.
text: If the data has no very large or very small values, the mean and the median are close, and either works.
If one or two values are extreme (like ₹300 pocket money among ₹50–₹70), use the median. The mean gets pulled towards the extreme value.
The mean need not be one of the data values (the mean of 2 and 3 is 2.5), but it always lies between the smallest and the largest value.

picture.caption: Choosing the representative value.

think.question: Marks: 35, 40, 38, 95, 37. Which describes a typical mark better?
think.answer: The median (38). The mean (49) is pulled up by 95.

lessons.aha: Extreme values pull the mean; the median stays in the middle.

lessons.title: Range: how spread out?
lessons.story: Batter A scored 20, 45, 30, 50, 35. Batter B scored 10, 90, 5, 60, 15. Both have mean 36. Who is more reliable?
text: Range = highest − lowest. A: 50 − 20 = 30. B: 90 − 5 = 85.
A smaller range means the values stay close together. A is more consistent, even though both have the same mean.

picture.caption: Same mean, very different spread.

think.question: Find the range of 12, 7, 20, 15.

lessons.aha: Range = highest − lowest. A small range means consistent data.

lessons.title: Telling the story of data
lessons.story: The maximum temperatures of a week are 31, 33, 30, 34, 32, 35, 29 °C. Anu writes a report for the class notice board.
text: Mean = 224 ÷ 7 = 32°C. Median (ordered middle) = 32°C. Range = 35 − 29 = 6°C.
Statistical statement: 'This week was warm, with a typical maximum of 32°C, and the days were similar (range 6°C).'

picture.caption: Daily maximum temperatures (°C).

think.question: Which is a better typical value when one value is extreme: mean or median?

lessons.aha: Describe data with a typical value (mean or median) and a spread (range).

examples.question: Mean of five is 12; four are 10, 14, 9, 15.

mistakes: Finding the median without ordering.
Taking only one middle value for an even count.
Dividing by the wrong count for the mean.
Calling range the highest value.
checklist: Write the ordered list.
Show the sum and the count.
State which value is better and why.
Give units.

notes.subtitle: Compass Constructions & Tessellations

concepts.title: Cutting a line exactly in half
concepts.text: Equal arcs from both ends cross on the perpendicular bisector.

concepts.title: Angles without a protractor
concepts.text: Same radius three times makes an equilateral triangle, which gives 60°. Bisect to halve an angle.

concepts.title: Parallel lines with compasses
concepts.text: Copy a corresponding angle to draw a parallel line.

concepts.title: Which tiles fit?
concepts.text: Shapes tile when their angles at each corner add up to exactly 360°.

method: For tilings, add the angles at a point.

example.question: Steps for the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps: Equal arcs from A and B above and below.

practice.question: Interior angle of a regular pentagon.
How many squares meet at a point in a tiling?
Bisect a 90° angle. What angle do you get?
Do 1 square + 2 octagons fit at a point?
Do 3 triangles + 2 squares fit at a point?
Show that 1 triangle + 2 dodecagons (150°) fit at a point.

tips: Fixed radius for each pair of arcs.
Tiles must total 360° at a corner.
notes.intro: Anu's school is laying a new floor with tiles. 'Why are tiles always squares or hexagons, and never pentagons?' she asks. Thatha answers with angles.
before: know the angle sum of a triangle and that angles round a point add to 360°

lessons.title: Drawing an eye with arcs
lessons.story: Anu's art teacher asks her to draw an eye shape using only compasses. 'Where do I put the compass point?'
text: Draw a line AB. With the point on A and a radius bigger than AB, draw an arc above B. With the point on B and the same radius, draw a matching arc. The two arcs make the upper eyelid.
Repeat below the line for the lower eyelid, and draw a small circle in the middle for the pupil. Every arc is part of a circle whose centre is the compass point.

picture.caption: Arcs from the two ends make an eye.

think.question: What stays the same along an arc?
think.answer: The distance from the compass point (the radius).

lessons.aha: Every arc is part of a circle. The compass point is the centre.

lessons.title: Cutting a line exactly in half
lessons.story: Anu must mark the exact middle of an 8 cm strip without measuring 4 cm.
text: Open the compasses to more than half the length. From A, draw arcs above and below the line. Keep the same opening and draw arcs from B. Join the two crossing points.
This line cuts AB in half at a right angle: it is the perpendicular bisector. Every point on it is the same distance from A and B.

steps: Arcs from A, above and below
picture.caption: Constructing the perpendicular bisector.

think.question: Why must the compass opening be more than half of AB?
think.answer: Otherwise the arcs from A and B do not cross.

lessons.aha: Equal arcs from both ends cross on the perpendicular bisector.

lessons.title: A right angle the Śulba-sūtra way
lessons.story: About 2,800 years ago, Indian builders made fire altars with exact right angles. They had no protractors, only ropes and pegs.
text: The Śulba-sūtras describe a rope with knots that divide it into 3, 4 and 5 equal parts. Stretch it into a triangle: the angle between the 3 and 4 parts is exactly 90°.
With compasses: to draw 90° at a point P on a line, mark two points at the same distance on both sides of P, then construct the perpendicular bisector of those two points. It passes through P at 90°.

picture.caption: A 3-4-5 rope triangle gives a right angle.

think.question: Would a rope triangle of 6, 8 and 10 parts also give 90°?
think.answer: Yes; it is the 3-4-5 triangle doubled.

lessons.aha: 3-4-5 triangles make right angles. Compasses can also build 90° with a perpendicular bisector.

lessons.title: Angles without a protractor
lessons.story: Ravi has no protractor, but he needs a 60° angle.
text: From the vertex O, draw an arc that cuts the arm at P. With the same opening, put the compass point on P and cut the arc at Q. ∠POQ = 60°, because O, P and Q make an equilateral triangle.
To halve any angle, draw equal arcs from the two points on its arms and join the vertex to where they cross. Halve 60° for 30°, and halve 90° for 45°.

picture.caption: OP = PQ = OQ, so the triangle is equilateral and ∠POQ = 60°.

think.question: How can you construct 120°?
think.answer: Step off the 60° arc twice along the circle.

lessons.aha: Same radius three times makes an equilateral triangle, which gives 60°. Bisect to halve an angle.

lessons.title: Copying an angle
lessons.story: Ravi must draw an angle exactly equal to one in his book, without a protractor.
text: With centre at the book angle's vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms. With the same radius, draw an arc from the start of your new ray.

Measure the gap between the two crossings on the book angle with your compasses. Use that gap to cut your new arc. Join the vertex to that point. The angles are equal, because the triangles are congruent (SSS).

steps: Same arc on the new ray
picture.caption: Copying an angle with compasses.

think.question: Why are the two angles equal?
think.answer: The two triangles have three equal sides (SSS).

lessons.aha: Same radius, same gap: the copied angle is exactly equal.

lessons.title: Parallel lines with compasses
lessons.story: Anu needs a line through point P parallel to line l.
text: Draw any line through P that crosses l. It makes an angle with l. Copy the same angle at P, in the same position (corresponding angle).
Equal corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel (Chapter 5).

picture.caption: Copying the 60° angle at P gives a line parallel to l.

think.question: Which angle rule makes this construction work?
think.answer: Equal corresponding angles mean parallel lines.

lessons.aha: Copy a corresponding angle to draw a parallel line.

lessons.title: Hexagons, stars and arches
lessons.story: Anu draws a circle and, keeping the same compass opening, steps around it. Exactly six steps fit!
text: The side of a regular hexagon equals the radius of its circle. Mark the six points and join them in order: a regular hexagon. Each angle at the centre is 60°.
Join every second point instead: two overlapping triangles make a six-pointed star. Arches in buildings are drawn with arcs from two centres on the base line.

picture.caption: Regular hexagons; each side equals the radius of its circle.

think.question: How many 60° angles make a full turn at the centre?

lessons.aha: The radius steps exactly 6 times around its circle, giving a regular hexagon.

lessons.title: Which tiles fit?
lessons.story: At a corner of the floor, several tiles meet at one point. Thatha says, 'The angles at that point must add up to exactly 360°, with no gap and no overlap.'
text: A regular polygon with n sides has each angle 180° × (n − 2) ÷ n. Triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°.
6 triangles: 6 × 60° = 360° ✓. 4 squares: 4 × 90° = 360° ✓. 3 hexagons: 3 × 120° = 360° ✓. Pentagons: 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so gaps appear.

picture.caption: Three hexagons meet at each corner: 3 × 120° = 360°.

think.question: Can regular octagons (135°) tile a floor alone?
think.answer: No. 360 ÷ 135 is not a whole number.

lessons.aha: Shapes tile when their angles at each corner add up to exactly 360°.

lessons.title: Tangrams
lessons.story: Thatha cuts a square of card into 7 pieces: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, a small square and a parallelogram. 'This is a tangram,' he says.
text: You can rearrange the 7 pieces into animals, people and boats. All the shapes have the same area as the original square, because no piece is lost.
The 2 large triangles together make half of the square. A small triangle is 1/16 of the square, and the small square, the parallelogram and the medium triangle are each 2 small triangles.

picture.caption: The 7 tangram pieces always make the same total area.

think.question: What fraction of the whole square is one large triangle?

lessons.aha: Rearranging pieces changes the shape but never the area.

lessons.title: Mixing tiles
lessons.story: Anu sees a floor with octagons and small squares. 'Two kinds of tiles together?'
text: At each corner: 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°. So 2 octagons and 1 square fit.
Other mixes: 2 triangles + 2 hexagons (60 + 60 + 120 + 120 = 360) and 3 triangles + 2 squares (180 + 180 = 360).

picture.caption: Mixed tiles work when the angles at a corner total 360°.

think.question: Do 1 triangle and 2 regular 12-gons (150° each) fit at a point?

lessons.aha: Any mix works if the angles at each corner total 360°.

examples.question: Steps for the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps: Equal arcs from A and B above and below.

examples.question: Interior angle of a regular octagon.
Line through P parallel to l.
steps: Copy the corresponding angle at P.

mistakes: Changing the compass width in the middle of a step.
Erasing construction arcs.
Using 180°(n − 2) without dividing by n.
Forgetting that angles at a point must total exactly 360°.
checklist: Keep arcs visible.
Write the steps of construction.
Show the 360° check for tilings.
Measure angles with a protractor to check.

notes.subtitle: Simple Linear Equations

concepts.title: An equation is a balance
concepts.text: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other side.

concepts.title: Solving step by step
concepts.text: Undo the last operation first. Check the answer by putting it back into the equation.

concepts.title: Letters on both sides
concepts.text: Move the letter terms to one side and the numbers to the other, using the same step on both sides.

concepts.title: From story to equation
concepts.text: Choose a letter, write the other quantities with it, form the equation, solve, then answer in words.

formulas: If a = b, then a + c = b + c, a − c = b − c, ac = bc, a/c = b/c (c ≠ 0)
method: Let the unknown be a letter.

practice.question: The sum of three consecutive numbers is 72. Find them.
A father is 30 years older than his son. In 5 years he will be 3 times as old. Find the son's age.
I think of a number, multiply it by 5 and subtract 12. I get 48. Find the number.
₹500 is shared between A and B so that A gets ₹80 more than B. Find each share.

notes.intro: Thatha puts 2 small bags of marbles and 9 loose marbles on one side of a balance, and 35 marbles on the other. The balance is level. 'How many marbles are in each bag?' he asks. This is the method of solving equations.

lessons.title: An equation is a balance
lessons.story: Both sides of Thatha's balance weigh the same. Anu writes what she sees: 2b + 9 = 35, where b is the number of marbles in one bag.
text: An equation says two sides are equal, just like a level balance. The letter is the unknown we want to find.
If you add or remove the same amount from both sides, the balance stays level. If you double or halve both sides, it still stays level.

picture.caption: Both sides weigh the same.

think.question: What happens if you remove 9 marbles from one side only?
think.answer: The balance tips. You must remove 9 from both sides.

lessons.aha: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other side.

lessons.title: Solving step by step
lessons.story: Anu removes the 9 loose marbles from both sides. Now 2 bags balance 26 marbles.
text: 2b + 9 = 35. Subtract 9 from both sides: 2b = 26. Divide both sides by 2: b = 13. Each bag has 13 marbles.
Undo the operations in reverse order. The equation added 9 last, so undo that first; then undo the ×2.

picture.caption: After removing 9 from each side: 2b = 26, so b = 13.

think.question: Solve 3x + 4 = 25.

lessons.aha: Undo the last operation first. Check the answer by putting it back into the equation.

lessons.title: Letters on both sides
lessons.story: Ravi solves 4x − 7 = 2x + 9. 'There is x on both sides!'
text: Remove 2x from both sides: 2x − 7 = 9. Add 7 to both sides: 2x = 16. So x = 8.
Check: 4 × 8 − 7 = 25 and 2 × 8 + 9 = 25. Both sides are equal, so x = 8 is correct.

picture.caption: Collect the letters on one side and the numbers on the other.

think.question: Solve 6x + 5 = 4x + 15.

lessons.aha: Move the letter terms to one side and the numbers to the other, using the same step on both sides.

lessons.title: Equations from matchstick patterns
lessons.story: Anu's row of squares uses 3n + 1 matchsticks (Chapter 4). She has 61 matchsticks. 'How many squares can I make?'
text: Write the equation: 3n + 1 = 61. Subtract 1: 3n = 60. Divide by 3: n = 20 squares.
Patterns give rules, and rules give equations. If the result is not a whole number, that number of sticks does not fit the pattern exactly.

picture.caption: n squares need 3n + 1 sticks.

think.question: Can exactly 50 sticks make a row of squares?
think.answer: 3n + 1 = 50 gives n = 49/3, not a whole number. No.

lessons.aha: Turn the pattern rule into an equation, then solve it.

lessons.title: From story to equation
lessons.story: 'A rectangle has a perimeter of 54 cm. Its length is 3 cm more than its breadth.' Anu writes a plan.
text: Step 1: let the breadth be b cm. Step 2: the length is b + 3. Step 3: perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth), so 2(b + 3 + b) = 54.
Step 4: 4b + 6 = 54, so 4b = 48 and b = 12. Step 5: answer in words: breadth 12 cm, length 15 cm.

picture.caption: Story → letter → equation → answer.

think.question: The sum of three consecutive numbers is 72. Find them.

lessons.aha: Choose a letter, write the other quantities with it, form the equation, solve, then answer in words.

lessons.title: Ages and money problems
lessons.story: Raju is 4 times as old as his son. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 60. How old are they now?
text: Let the son be s years. Raju is 4s. In 5 years: (s + 5) + (4s + 5) = 60.
5s + 10 = 60, so 5s = 50 and s = 10. The son is 10 and Raju is 40. Check: 15 + 45 = 60. ✓

picture.caption: A table keeps ages organised.

think.question: ₹500 is shared so that A gets ₹80 more than B. Find each share.

lessons.aha: Use a table for ages: add the same number of years to every person.

lessons.title: Making your own equations
lessons.story: Thatha says, 'Every equation is built from a simple truth.' He starts with x = 4.
text: Do the same thing to both sides: × 3 → 3x = 12. + 5 → 3x + 5 = 17. The equation 3x + 5 = 17 still has the solution x = 4.
Solving is just building in reverse: − 5 then ÷ 3 takes you back to x = 4.

picture.caption: Build an equation forwards; solve it backwards.

think.question: Build an equation with solution y = 2 using two steps.

lessons.aha: Doing the same thing to both sides builds equations; undoing it solves them.

lessons.title: Mind the mistake, mend the mistake
lessons.story: Ravi solved three equations and got them all wrong. Anu checks each step.
text: x + 5 = 9 → x = 9 + 5 is wrong: to remove +5, subtract 5 from both sides, so x = 4.
3x = 12 → x = 12 − 3 is wrong: 3x means 3 × x, so divide: x = 4.
2(x + 3) = 14 → 2x + 3 = 14 is wrong: 2 multiplies both terms, so 2x + 6 = 14 and x = 4.

picture.caption: Undo with the opposite operation.

think.question: Check x = 4 in 2(x + 3) = 14.

lessons.aha: Undo + with −, and × with ÷. Always check the answer in the original equation.

lessons.title: A pinch of history: the magic formula
lessons.story: Indian mathematicians like Brahmagupta solved equations more than 1,300 years ago. They described a rule that solves every equation of the form ax + b = c.
text: Start with ax + b = c. Subtract b: ax = c − b. Divide by a: x = (c − b) ÷ a. This works for any numbers a, b, c with a ≠ 0.

picture.caption: Remove b from both sides, then divide by a: x = (c − b) ÷ a.

think.question: Use the formula for 5x − 3 = 22.

lessons.aha: For ax + b = c, the solution is x = (c − b) ÷ a.
formulas: ax + b = c ⇒ x = (c − b) ÷ a

mistakes: Doing an operation on one side only.
Forgetting to multiply every term inside a bracket.
Sign errors when moving terms.
Not answering the actual question (for example giving b, when the length is asked).
checklist: Write 'Let … = x'.
Write each step on a new line.
Check by substitution.
Give units.
